text:
New adventure. 🚀
I've started a new company: Outlast AI

If we've been connected for a while,
you probably know this already:

I've been focused on growing Fonoster.
But building in Voice AI changed my perspective.

It made me ask the question:
Where can Voice AI make the biggest impact?

After dozens of conversations with leaders from Fortune 500 companies as well as small/medium businesses one thing became clear.

Procurement and supply chain are overdue for a revolution.

The opportunity?
Conversational AI.

Over the last few months, my friends and I have been quietly helping customers to:

⟡ Cut tens of thousands of dollars in workload and hiring costs.
⟡ Save 20+ hours per week per full time employee

This is early.
But the signal is strong.

I'm excited to keep talking with procurement leaders.

▶ Calling procurement leaders: If this resonates, let's talk!
notes: Highest-impression post in the trailing year. Use ONLY as a structural template for the 'new adventure' announcement format (hook -> context -> the opportunity -> proof bullets -> CTA). Not current positioning; do not reference the product by name when drafting.

text:
True story.
Someone asked me the other day:
"How much would you sell Fonoster for?"

I've been asked before.
And every time, I'm never really ready.

I paused.
Then I said:
"It will be some time before I'm ready."

Because truth is,
I'm ready, but it's not about money.
There's still too much fun ahead.

He said:
"Don't worry, it's just hypothetical."

This time I didn't hesitate.
I smiled and said:
"100 Million USD."

He laughed. Nervously.

Someone asked me the other day: What's the difference between Fonoster and Vapi, Bland, Retell, etc.?

I was like, what? Isn't it obvious?
Just kidding.

But here's the reality: most Voice AI vendors are simply an orchestration layer.

And it's really not that hard.
You've got:

↘ A speech-to-text engine
↘ A text-to-speech engine
↘ A bidirectional stream
↘ A state machine (Optional)

And voilà, you have Voice AI.

Fonoster also has an orchestration layer.
But it's so much more.

[Post includes an image of Fonoster's full surface: Domains, Agents, ACLs, Credentials, Secrets, API Keys, Monitoring, captioned 'The difference.']

text:
The Voice AI industry is in desperate need of 𝙆𝘼𝙍𝙈𝘼. 💡

⟡ Kamailio
⟡ Asterisk
⟡ RTPEngine
⟡ Monitoring (Homer)
⟡ ARI

This stack has been around for decades.
But it's still the heart of everything Voice, yes, including Voice AI.

It's hard to find people who deeply understand it.

You'll find an Asterisk pro, but never touched ARI.
RTPEngine? Maybe a handful.
Kamailio? You basically need to be an alien.
And ARI? That's just for the brave.

☑ But this gap is also an opportunity.

If you're in VoIP, now is the time to go wide.
To learn the full KARMA stack.
To build the Voice AI systems of tomorrow.

I'm gearing up to launch training and resources around KARMA to help fill the growing demand I'm seeing at Fonoster.

Voice AI is growing fast.
Let's make sure open-source talent grows with it.

▶ I'm building an Army of KARMA professionals. Reach out if your company needs help.

I've been thinking a lot about what it takes to win in Voice AI. ↓

The answer? Collaboration.
There's so much involved you just can't do it alone.

From the tech side, you need:

↳ Speech vendors
↳ Trunking providers
↳ Inference providers
↳ Third-party integrations

From the business side, you need:

✣ Infrastructure (Voice AI orchestration)
✣ Builders (agencies or developers)
✣ Partners (including VoIP providers)
✣ Educators and content creators
✣ Communities

Remove one link and the ecosystem collapses.
Add to it and you're almost guaranteed to thrive.

How are you contributing to the Voice AI ecosystem today?

▶ Fonoster is infra for Voice AI. Feel free to DM me.

text:
Is speech-to-speech the future of 𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐?
I'm not so sure. Not yet. ↓

The pitch sounds great:

✣ Low latency
✣ Simpler stacks
✣ Lower costs (someday)

It'll cover a lot of ground.
But here's the catch:

We give up too much.

↳ Can't swap out LLMs
↳ Can't bring your own voices
↳ Can't go beyond the box

And let's not forget:

↳ Few supported languages
↳ Locked pipelines
↳ No custom anything

For some, that's fine.
For others, it's a dead end.

▶ By the way, Fonoster is live at https://app.fonoster.com

text:
I spent more time than I admit duct taping 𝑲𝑨𝑹𝑴𝑨 in 2025. And I won't do it again.

Most voice companies run the same stack:

⟡ Kamailio
⟡ Asterisk
⟡ RTPengine
⟡ Monitoring with HOMER
⟡ ARI

Some of this software is decades old. And that's not a bad thing.

For most companies, KARMA is right. Almost every need is covered.
It's proven, documented, and battle-tested.
I use parts of it in Fonoster, and it works really well.

But things change at scale.
With millions of calls per day, cracks show.

Asterisk crashes without a clear reason. No real horizontal scalability.
RTPengine is great, but heavy and often too much.
Kamailio is still strong, but not friendly, and it's not fun.
Then come the bugs. Endless. Hard to reproduce.

The worst part? Most use cases didn't need KARMA.
I saw teams using Asterisk to get a bidirectional stream. That's it.

Too many stacks. Too much surface area. Too much duct tape.

𝐇𝐞𝐫𝐞'𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧.

KARMA is still the right choice. For most teams. For most problems.
But not all problems are telecom problems. If you only need streams, build for streams.

In 2026, I'm choosing less. Less legacy. Less glue. And far fewer midnight restarts.

▶ Connect with me to see what I'll be shipping for the rest of 2026.
notes: Contrarian-on-own-stack take: loves KARMA, argues most teams over-buy it. ~4.4k impressions (between #9 and #11 in the 365 ranking). 18 comments. Uses a bold-Unicode header mid-post.

text:
Confession: I suck at sales. So I retreat into building.
↓

Building used to be a comfort zone. The one thing engineer-founders are reliably good at.

And it was a great excuse.

"Revenue's flat? We need more features."

Nobody questions a founder who's building. It's the most socially acceptable place to hide.

Then a 6-month project started taking a week, and the excuse evaporated.

Sorry, friends. 𝘈𝘐 didn't just speed up building.
It exposed that building was never the bottleneck for guys like me. It was elsewhere.

Distribution. Sales. The room I kept avoiding.

So I'm done hiding behind the repo. I'm treating sales like a system I can debug:

⟡ one real outreach a day
⟡ track what gets replies
⟡ iterate like it's code

Still bad at it. Doing it anyway.

Engineer-founders: what do you build to avoid the thing you should be doing?
notes: Best example of the warm operator-journal voice register: vulnerable confession hook, engineer reframing ('debug sales'), engagement-question close. Lower raw reach but high-quality voice template.

text:
99% of phone systems are stuck in 1999.
↓

It's easy to think 𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐 is too crowded. The FOMO on LinkedIn is crazy.

But the reality is, we're early. Embarrassingly early.

Try this. Walk down a busy street in any big city. Write down the first 10 businesses you see. Then call them.

Surprise. You're talking to a 1999 tree-based IVR.

My estimate? Less than 1% of all calls made to a business today are answered by an actual voice agent.

It has nothing to do with the tech not being ready. It is.

The hard part is integrating with the systems already in place. Old PBXs. Crusty SIP trunks. Carriers that fight you on every change.

So today I just want to push back on one assumption: that you're too late.

You're not. You are embarrassingly early.

Are you building Voice AI for a brand-new use case, or fighting a legacy system?

PS: At Fonoster we are building QCobro to take on exactly one of those stuck-in-1999 use cases. Read more here → https://qcobro.com
notes: Strong stat-shock hook ('99% stuck in 1999') + the 'embarrassingly early' thesis. Recent (1mo). PS routes to QCobro.

text:
The future of AI isn't smarter models. It's encoding YOUR process into commands YOU can repeat. ↓

Why wait for the next model to fix your workflow?
I stopped and encoded mine.

My take on it is 𝘱𝘴𝘴𝘵𝘢𝘤𝘬: a Claude Code plugin for the things I do on repeat.

One command I run every morning is /𝐩𝐬:𝐤𝐚𝐢𝐳𝐞𝐧.
It does one thing. Make my code 1% better. Daily.

⟡ a missing test
⟡ a sharper type
⟡ a dead file removed
⟡ a flaky workflow, fixed

1% a day isn't 365% a year.
Compounded, it's ~37x.

The leverage was never the model being clever. It's the same small ask, every day, with the convention already encoded so it never drifts.

I say what "better" means. The machine does the reps.

▶ Steal the plugin: https://lnkd.in/eka7Yp3X

text:
𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐 has so many moving pieces.
Get one wrong, and the whole thing falls apart. ⤵

Six layers, one conversation:

⟡ SIP signaling
⟡ Bi-directional stream
⟡ Speech: STT + TTS
⟡ Language model
⟡ Orchestration
⟡ Agent mechanics

Everyone tunes the model.
But the stream is 70% of the work.
And the first thing to crack.

Full breakdown below ↓

Which layer broke first for you?

text:
Most 𝑉𝑜𝑖𝑐𝑒 𝐴𝐼 platforms have shockingly thin SIP support.

⤵

Everyone obsesses over the agents.
Almost nobody gets the layer underneath right.

Twilio did. A long time ago.

Their Elastic SIP Trunking nailed the part that actually breaks at scale: elasticity. No capacity planning. No pre-provisioned trunks. It just absorbs the load.

That's the piece I wanted in the open.

So that's what 𝘙𝘰𝘶𝘵𝘳 is.

A black-box implementation of most of what makes Elastic SIP Trunking great. Elasticity included.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗲𝘁:

⟡ Massive scale, built in
⟡ Most SIP scenarios, covered
⟡ No legacy PBX to babysit
⟡ Open source, yours to run

I'm convinced you shouldn't need a 20-year-old stack to ship modern voice. The carrier edge can be boring, elastic, and open. All at once.

That's the whole bet I'm making.

▶ I write about building voice without the legacy stack here: https://pedrosanders.me/
notes: Positions Routr against Twilio's Elastic SIP Trunking. gap-callout hook, bold-Unicode 'What you get' header, pedrosanders.me CTA.

The unglamorous infra is the part that lasts. Voice agents are easy to spin up in a weekend. Maintaining what runs underneath them is the real work, and that's where I keep showing up.

text:
What do you do when failure is not an option?
⤵

I think about this more than I like to admit.

What if revenue goes to zero tomorrow?
No pipeline. No safety net.

The best time to prepare is when you don't need it.

So I run a list in my head:

⟡ Sales conversations that went cold
⟡ A business area I know works, but don't love
⟡ Friends in the private sector
⟡ Co-founders I've met in my DMs
⟡ Family and close friends
⟡ How is my personal brand today?

Which door can I knock on today that at least buys me time?

And then something shifts.

I realize how much equity I actually have.
Not financial equity.
Relationship equity. Reputation equity. Trust equity.

I could unlock a dozen conversations this week if I had to.

I prefer to keep things at a sustainable pace.
But it's good to know that things will be ok.

What's your contingency list look like?

▶ Speaking of doors, I'm building automated collections for finance orgs. DM me if that's your world. https://qcobro.com

text:
Voice AI will feel like AGI when we learn to measure End of Thought (EoT.)

(Hint: Endpointing + VAD is not enough.)

In conversation, we pause and gather our thoughts.
We don't rush every sentence; we take our time.

↳ Today's Voice AI can't replicate this
↳ But the missing ingredient is EoT

Endpointing + VAD work, but it's not enough.

We get a lot of false positives.
And false negatives.

I don't have a solution yet.

But this is a big challenge.
↓

(IMO, the most critical challenge to solve in Voice AI)

Is anyone working on this problem?

Companies like Deepgram, Talkscriber, and Picovoice are well-equipped to address this problem.

What are your thoughts?

▶ Like and re-share to let me know this is relevant to you.
notes: High-comment (27) Educational/Industry hybrid. prediction-explainer hook ('will feel like AGI when...') + names real players (Deepgram, Picovoice) + open question. EoT/turn-taking is a recurring Pedro theme.

text:
𝑾𝒉𝒐 𝒘𝒊𝒍𝒍 𝒘𝒊𝒏 𝒕𝒉𝒆 𝑽𝒐𝒊𝒄𝒆 𝑨𝑰 𝒓𝒂𝒄𝒆?
(It's not who you think.)

And no, it's not infra either.

Here's the harsh truth:
Voice AI is converging. Fast.

Building features? Now a weekend project.

Everything above the telephony layer?
Easy to copy. Even easier to replace.

That's why every vendor feels the same. Just a different flavor.

⟡ Latency? Handled
⟡ Workflows? Baked in
⟡ SIP? Everyone's got it
⟡ MCP? Already shipped
⟡ Smart turn-taking? Getting there

Switching vendors? Just a prompt away.

So who will win?

→ The ones with a strong community
→ The ones with partnerships (think ccaas)
→ The ones deep in verticals
→ And yes, the agencies too

And you are not too late to join the race.
Just pick a niche.
Start building.

text:
The biggest pain in Voice AI is not what everyone thinks.

⤵

It's not LLM intelligence.
It's not turn-taking.
It's not even latency on a slide.

It's the infrastructure beneath all of it.

The boring stuff nobody demos:

⟡ SIP trunking that doesn't drop
⟡ Media servers that scale
⟡ DTMF that actually works
⟡ Compliance-grade recording
⟡ PSTN + carrier routing

𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐 demos win on a laptop.
Voice AI products die in production.

The gap between those two?

Not a smarter model.
A telephony stack.

And 90% of new builders have never touched one.

Most teams ship on infra they don't understand.
Hoping the pricing holds.
Hoping the SDK holds.
Hoping the SLA holds.

That bet ages badly.

The next 18 months of Fonoster get decided below the model.

Not above it.

What's the worst infra failure you've seen take down a voice agent in production?
notes: myth-bust hook + the 'demos win on a laptop, products die in production' line. Strong Industry Take; engagement-question close pulls war stories.

text:
Voice AI is being pitched for every industry on earth. Most of those bets won't pay back. ⤵

I've seen it all.

⟡ Voice AI for healthcare
⟡ Voice AI for defense
⟡ Voice AI for IoT
⟡ Voice AI for "the future of X"

Not every vertical strikes ROI the same way.

I'm betting on the boring ones. Where the agent either saves real money or makes real money for the customer. Today. Measurable on the next billing cycle.

That's why I'm building 𝙌𝘾𝙤𝙗𝙧𝙤.

A 𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐 collections agent for LATAM lenders.
Spanish-first. Built on 𝘍𝘰𝘯𝘰𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘳.

Why this market?

Take the Dominican Republic. The delinquency rate in microfinance is huge. Every lender has a recovery problem.

Every collections team is short-staffed, expensive, and capped by how many calls a human can make in a day.

That's not a "future of voice" pitch. That's a money problem today.

Pretty demos don't pay. Recovered loans do.

▶ See QCobro: https://qcobro.com/

text:
Most founders chase the biggest market they can imagine. I went the other way.

The next chapter of my journey is 𝘝𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘪𝘤𝘢𝘭 𝘝𝘰𝘪𝘤𝘦 𝘈𝘐.

And not just any vertical. The smallest niche, I still believe, can leave a mark. ↓

Why niche over big?

⟡ Proximity beats scale early
⟡ Language is a moat
⟡ Culture is a moat
⟡ A market you own > a market you rent

LATAM collections are unsexy. Spanish-first. Regulatory. Local.

That's the point.

Big platforms can't out-context me here.
Their playbook is English, US-first, and generic.

Mine is Dominican Spanish and LATAM compliance.

Deals here don't close on Zoom. They close in person, coffee in hand. Sometimes a beer.

The mark you leave on a small market is bigger than the dent you make in a giant one.

text:
Last night I sat down with a question I keep avoiding:

How can a solopreneur scale in 2026?

↓

I run a small operation. Most weeks, I'm buried in bookkeeping, meeting prep, GitHub issues, and Discord pings.

The work I should be doing gets neglected.

So I started looking harder at "𝘈𝘐-𝘯𝘢𝘵𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘤𝘰𝘮𝘱𝘢𝘯𝘺" content. High-level, it makes sense. In practice, there's no framework I trust.

N8N and similar tools seem to have missed the shift. Overkill. They don't resonate.

So I'm sketching my own take. Simple:

⟡ Input arrives (transcript, issue, receipt)
⟡ AI always pre-processes
⟡ Agent acts via documented skills
⟡ Triggered by schedule or webhook
⟡ Output is work + a trace
⟡ Trace stored (𝘷𝘊𝘰𝘯) to improve daily

The trace is the bet (vCon).

If every action leaves a structured record, the company gets better at what it does, day by day.

I'm convinced others are working on this. I'm taking my own swing.

If you've been thinking about the same problem, how would you sketch it?
notes: vulnerable-open Industry Take on the AI-native solo company + the vCon 'trace' idea (the same structured-record philosophy behind this post-pulse data store). Engagement-question close.

text:
A few weeks ago I kept building
until 4am. Not once. A habit.
↓

Part of it was pure excitement.
The other part: AI makes me faster.

More done in the same hours.
So I just... kept going.

Here's how the spiral works.

I open a terminal for one feature.
Halfway in, I spot a bug.
I chase it. Then another.

Look up. It's 4am again.

Fun? Yes. Sustainable? No.

So I stopped trusting willpower
and leaned on a system I built.

psstack, my Claude Code plugin:

✧ spot a bug or idea
✧ capture it, don't chase it
✧ log it to GitHub with /ps:issues-report
✧ add a priority, move on
✧ next session, run /ps:today
✧ it triages, easy wins first

The trick isn't more discipline
at midnight.

It's capturing the shiny thing
so it stops hijacking tonight.

Then blocking real time to build.
With AI doing the reps,
that block stays short.

And I still get a lot done.

The repos will always be open.
My sanity has a bedtime now.

Engineer-founders: what's your rule
for not letting a "quick fix"
eat the whole night?

text:
The legacy stack still runs my calls today.

It won't be in a year. ↓

When I started Fonoster,
the answer was always the same stack.

Proven. Documented. Battle-tested.
And carrying a pile of things
we no longer need.

Most of it was built
for a world that's gone:

✧ Protocols nobody dials
✧ Features from the PSTN era
✧ Config languages from the 90s
✧ Layers that fight scale
✧ Glue holding glue together

I'm not ripping it out overnight.
It still handles real calls today.

But the problem is simpler
than the stack admits.

It's streams.
At scale.
With low latency.

And we finally have better tools.
Rust. Go.
Built to run flat out,
not to babysit legacy.

So here's the plan.

Replace the old parts.
One piece at a time.
Lean, and built for massive scale.

Because Voice AI won't be a feature.
It'll be everywhere.
Every app. Every call. Every business.

And everywhere means scale
most voice infra was never built to survive.

Give me a year.

▶ I write about building voice without the legacy stack here:
https://pedrosanders.me

text:
We had two ways to reach a borrower behind on a microloan. In LATAM, WhatsApp is the obvious yes. We bet on Voice AI first. ↓

Most founders chase the biggest, sexiest market they can picture.

I went the other way. I picked the smallest one I could find.

Voice AI for collections. In the Dominican Republic. 🇩🇴

People call it untapped. Here's what they leave off the slide:

✧ Returns that don't excite a VC
✧ Data residency nobody's ready for
✧ Deals closed in person, over coffee
✧ CPaaS vendors have no DR numbers

None of that is a tech problem. It's a "nobody wants to do the hard, local work" problem.

But that's the whole bet.

We're SIP-first, so interconnection in-country is ours to run, not a support ticket we file.

If voice here were easy, someone with a bigger logo would already own it.

That difficulty is the moat.

WhatsApp is coming. Great channel, we'll ship it. But voice is where we start. It's where the work is, so it's where the edge is.

If you bet on a market everyone else called too small, what made you start there?
